If the laptop’s retail price is 15 percent or more below the average price for comparable spec laptops, it earns full marks for baseline value alignment, if it is between 5 percent below and 5 percent above the average, it earns 75 percent of the possible marks, if it is between 5 and 15 percent above the average, it earns half marks, and if it is 20 percent or more above the average for comparable specs, it earns no marks for that section. If it requires one adapter for a common peripheral it earns 75 percent, if it requires two or more adapters for routine use it earns half marks, and if it does not include a charger in the box at all it earns no marks for that sub-measure. Long-term cost of ownership also includes assessing the ease of repair and upgradeability, with laptops that allow users to replace the RAM, storage, and battery at home with standard tools, without voiding the warranty, earning full marks for that sub-measure. The remaining 15 points of the price category go to use-case specific value, which adjusts the score to reflect how well the laptop meets the needs of its target audience, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all standard. For example, a budget laptop priced under $500 intended for high school students who only need to write papers, browse the web, and attend virtual classes is not penalized for lacking a high-end graphics card or 4K display, as those features would add unnecessary cost for its target user, and instead earns marks based on how well it delivers on the core needs of its intended audience at its price point. Once all performance and price points are tallied, the total score translates to a clear performance and value rating that consumers can use to make purchasing decisions. A total score of 90 to 100 indicates an exceptional laptop that offers class-leading performance at an outstanding price point, with no major flaws that would detract from everyday use, and is a top recommendation for almost any user in its target audience. A score of 80 to 89 indicates a very good laptop that offers strong performance and solid value, with only minor drawbacks like slightly loud fan noise under load or a single missing port that most users can work around easily. A score of 70 to 79 indicates a good laptop that meets most basic needs at a fair price, but may have noticeable tradeoffs like shorter battery life or limited upgradeability that users should consider before purchasing, especially if they plan to use the laptop for more than 2 or 3 years. A score of 60 to 69 indicates a below-average laptop that either has lackluster performance for its price or is overpriced for the specs it offers, and is only recommended if it is on sale for at least 20 percent below its retail price to offset its shortcomings. A score below 60 indicates a poor value laptop that either has severe performance issues that make routine use frustrating, is drastically overpriced for its features, or both, and should be avoided by most consumers in favor of better options at the same price point. To ensure the rubric remains fair as technology evolves, all baseline spec averages and performance thresholds are updated every six months to account for new processor releases, drops in component prices, and shifts in standard consumer expectations, so a laptop that scored well two years ago is held to the same standard as new releases when re-evaluated for current purchase recommendations. Additionally, testers will adjust use-case priority rankings as consumer needs shift, for example, as more users rely on cloud storage for their files, local storage capacity may become a less heavily weighted factor for budget student laptops, while battery life and webcam quality for virtual classes may become more important, to ensure the rubric continues to reflect the actual needs of people shopping for laptops in the current market.

I froze when I was jogging my usual tree-lined suburban trail last Saturday, the kind of crisp fall evening where the air smells like wood smoke and crushed apple cider donuts from the farm stand at the trailhead. I’d been pushing for a new personal best, my breath coming in steady puffs and my workout playlist thumping in my earbuds, when a sharp, echoing CRUNCH from the thick underbrush 15 feet to my left ripped me right out of my rhythm.

I’d brushed off my best friend’s warning to carry protection on solo dusk jogs for months, but in that split second, I was suddenly grateful I’d stuffed a mini can of PEPPER SPRAY into the pocket of my running vest that morning on a whim. I ripped out my earbuds, my heart hammering so hard I could feel it in my fingertips, and squinted into the long, stretching shadows—until two glowing, amber eyes blinked back at me. For a split, panicky second, I thought it was a coyote, or even a lost black bear, like the ones the local parks department had been issuing alerts about all month. But then a massive 12-point buck stepped into the slanted orange glow of the setting sun, its antlers so wide they almost brushed the oak branches on either side of it.

I’d seen dozens of deer on this trail over the years, but never one this big, never one that didn’t bolt the second it caught a whiff of human sweat or cherry energy gel. I’d read a hiking blog the week prior that rutting season made male deer unpredictable, even aggressive, so I locked my knees and held perfectly still, not even daring to swallow too loud for fear of spooking him. For 10 whole seconds that felt like an hour, we stared each other down—until a plump, ripe ACORN dropped from the oak above his head and smacked him right between the ears. He flinched so hard he stumbled back a step, then tossed his head and bounded off into the underbrush, hooves thundering so loud they shook the carpet of fallen maple leaves at my feet.

I didn’t move for another 30 seconds, my lungs burning and my legs wobbly, until I remembered I’d stashed a pack of TRAIL MIX loaded with mini peanut butter cups in my vest as a post-jog reward, and the urge to dig it out to steady my nerves finally pushed me to unfreeze. I fumbled for my dimming HEADLAMP to light the last mile of the unlit trail, glancing up to see the bright, round FULL MOON peeking through the treetops, its silver glow turning the pine needles pale and ghostly. When I finally stumbled into the trailhead parking lot, I almost walked straight into a bright yellow sign the parks department had hammered into a post that morning that blared CAUTION: ACTIVE WILDLIFE — a warning I’d breezed right past an hour earlier, too focused on beating my personal best to glance up.

I laughed shakily as I unlocked my car, popping a peanut butter cup into my mouth and making a mental note to never again zone out so hard on a solo jog, and to always, always check the trail alerts before I laced up my sneakers. That split second of freezing wasn’t just fear—it was the sharp, sudden reminder that even the most familiar, boring local trail could hold a surprise big enough to stop me mid-stride.

When Elias turned back with the book, Maren was staring at him, wide-eyed, like she’d just seen a ghost. “You didn’t… say anything,” she said, tilting her head, like she was trying to figure out if he was being polite or if he just hadn’t noticed. “About the tic, I mean.” Elias shrugged, setting the book on the table and pushing it toward her. “My cousin has Tourette’s. The first time Maren invited Elias to join her for a volunteer planting day, he’d spent 45 minutes the night before picking out work clothes that didn’t look like he’d tried too hard, settling on faded gray work pants and a frayed navy flannel he’d owned since his sophomore year of college. He’d even bought a new pair of work boots, because his old sneakers were full of holes and he didn’t want to step on a thorn or a piece of broken glass in the vacant lot. The planting day was cold and drizzly, the kind of soft Portland rain that seeps through your jacket before you even notice it’s falling, and when Elias arrived, Maren was already there, surrounded by a dozen teens from the local high school’s environmental club, passing out trowels and packets of milkweed seeds. She was wearing a neon yellow rain jacket with “Save the Bees” printed on the back, her hair pulled back in a messy braid dotted with dandelion petals, and she waved so hard when she saw him that she dropped the stack of seed packets she was holding. The teens didn’t even glance up when she jerked her shoulder and yelled “DANDELION!” as she knelt to pick up the seeds, just kept chatting and laughing as they dug holes in the soft, damp dirt. Elias learned that day that all the teens in Maren’s program were kids who’d been labeled “difficult” by their schools: some had ADHD, some were autistic, some had anxiety, all of them had been told they were too loud or too distracted or too “much” for traditional classroom settings. She said the plants never judged her, never asked her to be quieter or calmer or different, so she’d decided to build a space where kids could feel the same way. By the end of the planting day, Elias’s knees were muddy, his hands were blistered, and he’d helped plant 72 milkweed shoots and 40 native wildflower plugs, and he’d had more fun than he’d had in years. After the teens left, Maren suggested they get tacos at the food truck down the street, the one with the vegan al pastor that she swore was the best in the city. He snickered, nudged the friend sitting next to him, and said loud enough for both of them to hear, “Can’t she control that? Jesus, people will bring anything out in public these days.” Maren’s face fell, and she stared down at her taco, suddenly quiet, like she was used to comments like that, like they still stung even after all these years. Elias didn’t yell at the man, didn’t make a big scene, didn’t even look at him. He just moved his chair a few inches to the right, so he was sitting between Maren and the man, and asked her to tell him more about the tiny blue mason bees she’d been talking about earlier, the ones that nested in the hollow stems of raspberry bushes. Maren looked up at him, her eyes a little shiny, and started talking again, slowly at first, then faster, getting excited as she explained how mason bees were better pollinators than honeybees for native plants. When they finished their tacos, Elias ordered her an extra side of guacamole, her favorite, and they walked back to his apartment, their boots squelching in the rain puddles on the sidewalk. Maren knelt down to pet her, and when she snapped her fingers three times, a motor tic she got when she was happy, Mabel just nudged her hand for more pets, completely unfazed. They kissed for the first time that night, halfway through a song about clouds, and mid-kiss, Maren jerked her shoulder and chirped “CLOVER!” so close to his ear that it made him laugh. He pulled back, grinning, and said “That’s a good one. I like clover.” Maren laughed too, a little shaky, like she’d been worried he’d pull away or be weirded out, and she kissed him again, harder this time. Maren would come to the library during his shifts, sit at the reading table and press flowers for the library’s new botanical display, and leave sticky notes with bee jokes on his desk when she left. Elias would go to her planting days every Saturday, bring donuts for the teens, and carry extra water bottles and band-aids in his backpack for anyone who needed them. Elias’s sister teased him that he was smitten, that he’d turned into one of those guys who talks about his girlfriend every five minutes, and he didn’t even deny it.

### Section 3
Maren got the email inviting her to be the keynote speaker at the Pacific Northwest Native Pollinator Summit on a Tuesday, right as she was leaning against the front desk of the rare book room, telling Elias about the baby bumblebee queen she’d spotted in the lot off 28th Avenue that morning. But Maren was terrified. She told Elias about the last time she’d given a public talk, back when she was in college, speaking to a small class of 20 environmental science students. Maren thought for a minute, then shrugged, saying she didn’t know, that she wanted to do the talk, wanted the grant more than anything, but she was so scared of humiliating herself that she wanted to say no. Elias came up with a plan that night, after they’d eaten takeout pasta and watched a documentary about bees. They’d practice the talk every night for a month, in the rare book room after closing, when the library was empty and quiet. ### Section 4
The conference ballroom was packed when Maren and Elias walked in, full of people in blazers and hiking boots, carrying reusable water bottles covered in environmental advocacy stickers, chatting and laughing as they found their seats. The stage was at the front of the room, draped in green cloth, with a podium and a big screen set up for Maren’s slideshow, and a microphone sitting on the podium, glinting under the bright lights. He told her he wanted to spend the rest of his life planting milkweed with her, eating burnt toast on Sunday mornings, counting tics like they were constellations, listening to her yell random plant names across the library. When he finished, Maren said yes again, this time soft and steady, no tic, and then immediately snapped her fingers three times and yelled “CLOVER!” like she couldn’t help it, and Elias kissed her, right there on the hotel room floor, with Mabel (who they’d brought along in a carrier) watching them from the nightstand. They got married six months later, in the first pollinator corridor they’d planted together, surrounded by 30 of their closest friends and family, and bumblebees buzzing in the milkweed all around them. Maren wore a dress made of organic cotton, dotted with wildflower prints, and Elias wore a suit with a bumblebee boutonniere. Leo was the best man, and during his toast, he yelled “MINECRAFT!” mid-sentence, and everyone laughed, because by then all their friends and family were used to tics, used to random outbursts, used to rolling with it. Maren’s maid of honor, her cousin who also had Tourette’s, yelled “MILKWEED!” during her toast, and everyone yelled it back, like it was a cheer. A year after the wedding, they adopted a tiny terrier mix they found wandering around one of the pollinator corridors, and named her Clover, after Maren’s favorite tic. They bought a small house with a big front yard, which they turned into a mini pollinator garden, full of milkweed and wildflowers and bee hotels. Elias still works at the library, and Maren’s pollinator corridor program now has 12 part-time staff and 50 regular teen volunteers, and they’ve planted 32 corridors across the city. Every Tuesday, Maren still comes into the rare book room, brings Elias a jar of jam, and sits at the reading table, pressing flowers for the library’s displays. Every time she ticcs a plant or bug name, Elias writes it down in a small leather notebook, and at the end of every year, they make a print of all the names, framed with pressed flowers, to hang on their living room wall. Elias still has that first monarch butterfly sticker Maren gave him, now stuck to the lid of their wedding ring box, tucked in the back of his sock drawer. He thinks sometimes that people talk about love being grand, sweeping gestures, fancy dinners and expensive trips and big speeches. But for him, love is extra guacamole when strangers are rude, glittery signs that say “BUMBLEBEES RULE,” counting spatula flips on Sunday mornings, and a woman who yells plant names when she’s happy. It’s messy, and loud, and a little unorthodox, and it’s perfect, just like Maren.

thread: the day i learned the earth isn’t flat didn’t happen in science class or on a bleary 2 a.m. youtube deep dive.
it happened behind a dilapidated rest stop off i-40 in west texas, next to a dumpster that reeked of pickled eggs and expired gas station hot dogs.
i was hiding from a crew of roving birthday clowns who’d tried to trade me a squeaky rubber chicken for my last bag of flamin’ hot cheetos.
a guy in a mold-stained raincoat caked with pecan shell dust leaned against the dumpster next to me, chewing something that crunched way too loud.
he didn’t even glance my way when he said you know the flat earth thing’s bullshit, right? like he was commenting on the dusty wind.
i blinked, because i’d spent the last three months deep in flat earth tiktok just to annoy my cousin who works a desk job at nasa.
i mumbled yeah, duh, obviously, even though i’d spent the week prior arguing that gravity was just a network of giant magnets buried under the dirt.
he spit a pecan shell into the dumpster and held out a crumpled map that looked like it had been chewed by a very determined raccoon.
the map wasn’t the flat disc with the ice wall i’d seen a hundred times online, it was all lumpy, like a squashed orange someone had sat on through a road trip.
he said he’d spent the last twelve years driving every potholed back road in the continental u.s. selling home-roasted pecans out of his beat-up minivan.
he said if the earth was flat, he’d have driven off the edge somewhere near el paso back in ‘18, when his gps died and he drove straight for three whole days.
i squinted, because that didn’t line up with the lore everyone shared online, right? the ice wall was guarded by penguins with tiny tasers, everyone knew that.
he laughed so hard he snort-laughed, and a half-chewed pecan chunk flew out of his nose and landed right on the toe of my scuffed white sneaker.
he pulled out a crinkled polaroid of him standing on a rocky beach in chile, next to a penguin that was definitely not holding a taser, just a very tiny silver fish.
he said he’d sailed across the atlantic the year prior to sell pecans to a convent of nuns in portugal who were obsessed with his salted roast.
he never hit an ice wall on that trip, he said, just a flock of very aggressive seagulls that stole half his snack supply mid-voyage.
i thought about all the nights i’d stayed up arguing with strangers online that lunar eclipses were just a giant shadow cat crossing the face of the sun.
i thought about how my nasa cousin had sent me a printed photo of the earth from the international space station for my birthday, and i’d mailed it back to her with “photoshop” scrawled across it in crayon.
i thought about the time i tried to dig a hole to the “bottom of the flat disc” in my backyard and only hit a sprinkler pipe that flooded my entire patio.
the pecan guy handed me a handful of warm, salted pecans and said people love believing weird shit because it makes the world feel smaller, easier to hold.
i nodded, because that quiet, offhand line hit way harder than any textbook or snarky debunk video ever had.
the clowns from earlier yelled my name from the rest stop parking lot, waving the rubber chicken over their heads like a battle flag.
the pecan guy winked, climbed into his van that had “pecan pete’s world famous nuts” painted on the side in chipped neon pink, and drove off.
i never saw him again, but i still have that crumpled lumpy map tucked in the glove box of my car, right next to my expired registration.
i texted my cousin that night and told her she was right about the earth not being flat, and she sent back twelve clown emojis and a link to a nasa merch store.
i still don’t fully trust big gravity, though, just in case the giant magnet thing is partially true.
and i still side-eye any penguin i see at the zoo, just in case the tiny taser lore was less of a lie than the flat disc was.
